steps.title: Quantifiers
steps.html:
CountableUncountable
QuestionHow many lemons?How much rice?
A big amounta lot of / many lemonsa lot of / much rice
A small amounta few lemonsa little rice
Less than you neednot enough lemonsnot enough rice
More than you needtoo many lemonstoo much rice

a lot of works with both, so it is the safe choice in a positive sentence.

much and many are most natural in negatives and questions: We don't have much time.

too means it is a problem: too much salt is not a good thing.

steps.title: Saying numbers
steps.html:
TypeHow to say it
Fractions¼ a quarter · ⅓ a third · ½ a half · ¾ three-quarters
Percentages15% fifteen per cent · 4.7% four point seven per cent
Decimals2.89 two point eight nine · 0.3 nought point three
Temperatures22°C twenty-two degrees Celsius · −7°C minus seven
Big numbers3,000,000 three million

After the decimal point, say each figure separately: 2.89 is two point eight nine.

million has no -s after a number: three million people.

steps.title: You are going to read a recipe and some food facts.
steps.sub: How much of its own food do you think a small country grows?

steps.title: 1 · Plov for four
steps.html:
You need a kilo of rice, half a kilo of beef, four carrots, two onions and a little oil. That's all.

First, chop the onions and the carrots. Then heat the oil in a big pan and fry the beef for ten minutes. Add the onions and the carrots, and a little salt — not too much. Next, add the rice and enough water to cover everything. Boil it, then cook it slowly for forty minutes. Don't mix it. Finally, serve it hot with a few pieces of bread.

steps.title: 2 · And where does it come from?
steps.html:
Not many countries grow all of their own food. Singapore grows less than ten per cent of it: there isn't enough space, so almost everything arrives by ship. Papua New Guinea is the opposite — it grows about three-quarters of its food, and less than a quarter of its people live in cities.

Indonesia is the third largest rice country in the world. Forty million Indonesians work on farms, which is about a sixth of the population. And even Indonesia still imports three million tonnes of rice a year.
